tagline.text: Cebu's provincial history museum in a restored old jail

location.label: Location
location.text: M.J. Cuenco Avenue, Barangay Tejero, Cebu City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–900 (per person, covering local transport, admission and meals)

children.text: Museo Sugbo is Cebu's provincial history museum, opened in 2008 in the old Cebu provincial jail, which was begun in the 1870s. It brings together the Spanish and American colonial periods, the revolution and wartime records in one place, which makes it a good stop on a downtown Cebu City sightseeing day.

Museo Sugbo means "Cebu Museum." It is a history museum owned by the Cebu provincial government on M.J. Cuenco Avenue (Barangay Tejero) in Cebu City, close to Plaza Independencia and Fort San Pedro, so it fits easily into a walking route downtown. The building was originally the Cárcel de Cebú, the Cebu jail, designed in 1869 by the Spanish architect Domingo de Escondrillas, with construction starting around 1871. Many of its coral-stone blocks are believed to have come from the Parian church, which was demolished in 1878. The provincial government opened the museum on August 5, 2008 with its first four galleries.

The history of the building is part of the exhibition. A renovation ordered in 1892 added buildings behind the main structure, and the first six galleries are now housed in those rear buildings. The date of the second storey is unclear, but its design suggests the American colonial period. During the Philippine Revolution, many Katipuneros were jailed without trial and later executed at the nearby Carreta cemetery. In the early American period the building served as a stable for horses at the nearby racetrack before returning to use as a city and provincial prison. During the Japanese occupation, guerrillas tortured by the Kempeitai were held here, and after the war collaborators were jailed. From the 1950s to 1976 the front section was the city jail and three rear structures were the provincial jail; the facility was renamed the Cebu Provincial Detention and Rehabilitation Center (CPDRC) in the 1980s and emptied when it moved to a new complex in December 2004. In 2008 the provincial government moved the detention center to Kalunasan and turned this compound into a museum. Many items are on loan from or donated by private individuals and institutions. One travel blog calls it the largest museum in Cebu, and a heritage expert has said that for Cebu history up to World War II there is nowhere else to go.

Exhibits kept growing after the opening. According to Wikipedia, a Spanish-era well was unearthed in 2009 during work on the rear complex, and on August 13, 2009 Governor Gwendolyn Garcia and Dr. Ambeth Ocampo, then chair of the National Historical Institute, unveiled a National Historical Marker. The same day the Visayas Branch of the Museum of Philippine Political History and the National Museum Cebu Branch galleries opened, along with special exhibitions on Sen. Vicente Rama and on Gregorio and Jovito Abellana, and the Well of Good Fortune and Happiness was inaugurated, bringing the total to 10 galleries. These records date from around 2010, so the current lineup may differ.

This guide is for travelers spending a day or half a day in Cebu City who link the Basilica del Santo Niño, Magellan's Cross and Fort San Pedro into one route. According to Freeman and SunStar reports in August 2025, the museum closed for about two years and reopened to the public on August 29, 2025, while some sections damaged in the 2013 earthquake remain under rehabilitation with restricted access. The same reports gave general admission as ₱50 and ₱25 for students, with the museum open Monday to Friday. At the reopening, a marker designating the museum an Important Cultural Property, a status the National Museum granted two years earlier, was unveiled, and a Conservation Management Plan is under way, with full rehabilitation estimated at ₱5–10 million. There was also a report of a free-admission day on May 18, 2026 for International Museum Day, which shows how often policies change. Fees and hours cited from 2012 are out of date, so check just before you go.

This coral-stone building was designed in 1869 and begun around 1871, and its stone is said to be recycled from the Parian church. High fences, thick walls, a pair of ornate cannons at the entrance and a welcome fountain recall its jail days. The open quadrangle was once the venue for performances by the Cebu Dancing Inmates.

This gallery introduces island society before Spanish rule. It displays millet grains (kabog) used in the Cebuano dish budbod kabog and a replica of the 13th-century Golden Tara of Agusan; the original is at the Field Museum in Chicago.
This gallery covers Cebu under Spanish rule after Magellan's arrival in 1521. It is a good primer before you see the Basilica del Santo Niño, Magellan's Cross and Fort San Pedro nearby.

blocks.title: Katipunan collection and American period gallery

children.text: It covers the Philippine Revolution and the American occupation, and it carries extra weight because this building held Katipuneros without trial during the revolution. The Visayas Branch of the Museum of Philippine Political History shows materials on national heroes and women of the revolution, plus an old campaign poster for Manuel Quezon and Sergio Osmeña.

You will see bayonets, bombs, antique machine guns, bullets, rations, uniforms, World War II medals including the Purple Heart, and 1941 emergency currency issued by the Philippine National Bank. It shows what Cebu went through during the Japanese occupation through real objects.

Highlights include porcelain and Thai and Vietnamese ceramics excavated at Plaza Independencia during the SRP tunnel construction, coins and artifacts from the sunken galleon San Diego, a gold death mask of thin etched gold sheets, and a pre-colonial skull with a flattened forehead. Photography is not allowed in this gallery.

"Amidst Two Wars" displays the memorabilia of Gregorio and Jovito Abellana, and "Politics and Publishing" shows the memorabilia of Sen. Vicente Rama. They are worth a look if you are interested in Cebu's political and press history.

blocks.title: Visayan saints and Cebu media gallery

children.text: "Handumanan" is a collection of Visayan saints from the Rosita Arcenas Collection, and the Cebu media gallery covers the history of the local press. Ask locally whether they are currently on view.

items.title: Half-day downtown route
items.subtitle: The museum and the historic district

children.text: Take a taxi, Grab or jeepney from your Cebu City hotel to Museo Sugbo on M.J. Cuenco Avenue. A weekday morning is the safest bet.
See the ornate cannons and fountain at the entrance, buy a ticket and follow the galleries in chronological order.
Go through the pre-colonial, Spanish period, Katipunan and war galleries in turn.
See the finds from Plaza Independencia and the gold death mask in the National Museum Cebu branch. Photography is not allowed.
Have lunch at a nearby restaurant.
Head to Fort San Pedro, Magellan's Cross and the Basilica del Santo Niño.
Browse Carbon Market or Colon Street, then return to your hotel.
Opening hours differ by source, so ask before you arrive. The 2025 reopening reports said it is open Monday to Friday.
There are several direct flights every day from Manila Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB), taking about
1 hour 30 minutes
. Airlines and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
From the airport to downtown by taxi or Grab takes
30–60 minutes
depending on traffic.
Wikipedia lists jeepney routes passing nearby: 01K (Urgello), 02B (Pier), 03A, 03B and 03L (Mabolo), 10H (Bulacao, Pardo) and 22D (Mandaue).
Bus routes MB (SM City Cebu, SM Seaside City, Anjo World) and KMK (Minglanilla, Naga) are also listed. Routes change, so confirm locally.
In the city, a taxi or Grab is the simplest option. Parking is reported to be along the street. If the name is hard to pronounce, say "Museo Sugbo, MJ Cuenco."
The museum is described as four blocks from Plaza Independencia. Take a taxi if it is hot or raining.
The exhibits are mostly indoors, so rain does little harm to your plans, but there is some walking downtown, so the dry season is better.

The museum may hold events such as free admission around its August 5 anniversary (opened in 2008) and International Museum Day on May 18. A free day on May 18, 2026 was reported, so check if your dates match.

Downtown Cebu City hotels are concentrated around Fort San Pedro and Colon Street, and near IT Park and Ayala Center. The museum is easy to reach by taxi from anywhere in the city, so where you stay matters little.

There is no food outlet inside the museum; officials were considering adding one, according to a 2025 report. Have lunch nearby. Around Carbon Market and on Colon Street there are many local restaurants and street food stalls.
Admission and hours differ by source, so contact the provincial government or the museum before you go. The 2025 reports said open Monday to Friday, ₱50 general and ₱25 for students.
You can take photos without flash in most galleries, but photography is not allowed in the National Museum branch gallery.
Allow 2–3 hours to see everything at a relaxed pace. The galleries are reported to be air-conditioned with Wi-Fi.
Some security guards double as informal guides and are described as knowledgeable about the artifacts.
Combining it with Fort San Pedro, Magellan's Cross and the Basilica del Santo Niño in one route is efficient.
Areas damaged in the 2013 earthquake may be off limits, so follow staff instructions.
It is an old jail with stairs and narrow passages, and the floor may be uneven, so wear comfortable shoes.
Admission, hours and exhibits may have changed since the 2025 reopening. Check official notices just before you visit.
Some areas are under repair after the 2013 earthquake and are off limits.
Reports mix "open Monday to Friday" with other accounts of Monday or Sunday closures, so a weekday morning visit is the safest.
The old jail section has dark passages.
Watch for pickpockets downtown and carry your belongings in front of you.
Parking is only along the street, so bringing a car takes extra time.
An old Spanish fort on the downtown waterfront, at Plaza Independencia. Wikipedia describes the museum as four blocks from the plaza.
An iconic cross near Cebu City Hall that fits well into the same history route as the museum.
Cebu's oldest church, which draws many pilgrims.
A house museum showing how wealthy Cebuano families lived in the 19th century.
One of Cebu's oldest traditional markets, where you can see local life.
